newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai central bank says no new 1996/97 budget cut.
newsitem.headline: Thai central bank says no new 1996/97 budget cut.

text.p: Thai central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Monday Thailand would not resort to additional budget cuts to help balance its 1996/1997 budget but it will raise some taxes to offset falling tax revenue.

Rerngchai told reporters after meeting top economic planners that the government would likely raise at least three to four types of taxes this year and in 1998 to raise funds for making up for its revenue shortfalls. He did not elaborate.

The governor's statement was in line with earlier remarks by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan who said further budget cuts would aggravate the bearish Thai economy which is projected to grow about five to six percent, its slowest pace in 10 years.
The governor said the government would likely end the 1996/1997 (October/September) fiscal year with a small budget deficit. Thailand has reported a budget surplus every year for the past nine years.

Amnuay in March pushed through the cabinet his proposal for a 59 billion baht ($2.27 billion) reduction of this year's budget. He said last Friday a planned 1,008 billion baht government expenditure for 1997/1998 would also be trimmed by 26 billion baht.
Governor Rerngchai said he sees room for high Thai interest rates to ease later this year when the economy gains more stability and sluggish exports pick up.
Current prime lending rates, averaging 13.00-13.25 percent, are among the highest in the region.
The central bank has long adopted a policy of keeping domestic interest rates high to attract foreign capital and discourage speculation against the baht.
